title: Stable chooser protocol for model references (tag / semver / commit-hash)
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary:
This ticket defines the "stable chooser" protocol: a deterministic resolver algorithm and client-facing SDK surface for selecting a model variant when users reference models by tag, semver range, or commit hash. Goal is predictable, auditable resolution behavior across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments and to minimize surprise rollouts when tags or semver ranges move.

Resolution priorities (deterministic precedence):
1) Exact commit hash (sha): absolute match, winner. Used by heavy-production customers wanting bit-for-bit reproducibility. Resolver must validate object existence and digest match.
2) Exact semver version (vX.Y.Z) if provided: resolves to the canonical release artifact.
3) Semver range (e.g., ^1.2.0, >=2.0 <3.0): resolver selects the highest compatible released semantic version in the chosen channel (stable > rc > beta), honoring pre-release rules unless the range explicitly allows them.
4) Annotated/immutable tags (stable-2026-02-01, release-2026.02): if tag metadata contains an immutable ref (sha), resolve to that sha. Tags with stability annotations are treated preferentially over floating tags.
5) Floating tags ("latest", "dev", user-created ephemeral tags): resolved at request-time to current head of the tag; resolver records the resolved sha and returns it in response metadata with TTL and resolved_at.

Fallback and grace behavior:
- If a higher-precedence selector is missing (e.g., semver range matches zero versions), the resolver attempts the next rule only when explicitly allowed by the client via "allow_fallback=true". Default behavior is to fail with a clear error and suggest alternatives.
- Floating tags include a server-side TTL (default 5 minutes) that the console and SDKs expose. SDKs may cache resolution for TTL but must re-resolve on mismatch errors.
- For semver ranges where multiple releases have identical major/minor but differing performance profiles, resolver prefers the release with the highest compatibility score (heuristic combining performance-profile stability, release age, and explicit channel). The compatibility score is computed server-side and surfaced in metadata.

Client SDK surface changes (backwards-compatible):
- New request parameter: "model_ref" accepts three forms: "myorg/mymodel@sha:abcdef...", "myorg/mymodel@v1.2.3", "myorg/mymodel@^1.2.0" and tag forms "@stable-2026-02" or "@latest".
- Optional flags: "allow_fallback" (boolean), "prefer_immutable_tags" (boolean), "resolution_ttl_seconds" (integer) to control local caching. These flags are optional and default to server-safe values.
- Response fields (returned for all resolved requests): "resolved_sha", "resolved_version", "resolved_selector_type", "resolved_at", "compatibility_score", "resolution_channel". SDKs must expose these in the response object and include them in telemetry.

Performance profile publishing interplay:
- Every published performance profile must be bound to a sha. When a semantic or tag-based selector resolves to a sha, the runtime attaches the associated performance_profile_id to the model::serving-metrics record.
- If a semver range resolves to multiple candidate releases during off-line analysis, the console will surface the performance-profile delta between candidates and recommend a conservative default.

Rollback and canary rules:
- If a model version passes canary but is later marked 'regression' in the console, the resolver will continue to return the previously stable sha for semver ranges where compatibility_score drops below the stability threshold.
- For floating tags the platform supports a two-step 'pinned promotion' flow: create immutable annotated tag pointing at sha -> switch semantic tag mapping to annotated tag. This prevents accidental drift.

Observability and auditability:
- Every resolution decision is logged (selector, caller identity, resolved_sha, compatibility_score, reason) to the audit log.
- The console exposes a per-request resolution trace and a weekly report of selector churn (how often floating tags moved and semver range resolutions changed).

Migration guidance for customers:
- For production: prefer sha or exact semver. If using ranges, pin critical routes to resolved_sha after successful deployment (SDK helper: set "pin_after_resolution=true" to cache server-resolved sha as a route override).
- For rapid iteration: use annotated tags with stability windows (e.g., stable-2026-03) and only move semver ranges after perf/regression checks pass.

Edge cases and safety nets:
- Transitive model references (model A references model B by tag): resolver computes full closure and rejects resolution if any reference has a mismatched major ABI (compatibility_score < threshold) unless "force" is explicit.
- Private deployments: control-plane-less on-prem resolvers will use local tag-to-sha cache and a periodic signed manifest fetch mechanism (signed by Redwood) to validate shas.

Open questions (for review):
- Exact default values for resolution TTL and stability thresholds. Proposed defaults: TTL=300s, stability_threshold=0.85.
- UX for exposing compatibility scoring components in public docs vs. keeping as internal heuristics.

Acceptance criteria:
- Implementation: server resolver implements priority rules and emits resolution metadata.
- SDKs (JS/Python/Go): accept new flags and surface response metadata.
- Console: visible trace for at least 7 days and selector-churn dashboard.
- E2E: existing customer integration tests validate that pinned shas are immutable and that semver ranges resolve deterministically in CI (seeded with a reproducible manifest).
